title: How Animals Talk
summary: How animals such as monkeys, elephants, bees, ants, and Arabian wolves use sounds, movements, and smells to send each other messages.
poll: Animals can share messages almost as well as people can.

versions.title: Animal Talk
versions.text:
Can a monkey talk? Not with words. But it can send a signal. A signal is a kind of note. Some are sounds. Some are moves. Some are smells.

Some monkeys live in Africa. They have a call for each danger. One call means a big cat. The monkeys run up a tree. One call means an eagle. They look up. They hide in the bush. One call means a snake. They stand up tall. They look down at the grass.

Elephants make deep sounds. Some are too low for us to hear. But they go far. An elephant far off can get them.

A bee can dance. The dance shows where to find food. It shows how far to fly.

Ants leave a scent. It makes a trail to the food. The rest of the ants smell it. They walk on the trail.

Wolves live in Saudi Arabia. A wolf howls. The howl calls the pack. It tells strange wolves to keep out.

Animals warn. They find food. They find their kin. Men and women in labs record the sounds. They want to learn what each one means.

A honeybee can dance in its hive. The dance shows the other bees where to fly for food. It shows how far to go.

Ants leave a scent on the ground. The scent makes a trail. Other ants smell the trail. They follow it to the food.

Wolves live in the deserts of Saudi Arabia. A wolf howls to call its pack. The howl tells other wolves to keep away.

Animals use signals to warn, to find food, and to find each other. Scientists record the sounds. They want to learn what each one means.

versions.text:
Animals cannot speak with words, yet they communicate with one another constantly, exchanging messages that scientists call signals. These signals take many forms, because some are sounds, others are movements, and still others are chemicals that nearby animals can detect and follow.

Vervet monkeys in Africa produce a distinct alarm call for each type of predator, and researchers have learned to interpret what each vocalization means. When one monkey gives the leopard call, the entire group races up into the trees, but when it gives the eagle call, the monkeys look up at the sky and dive into thick bushes. A third call warns of a snake, so the monkeys stand on their back legs and carefully examine the ground. Because every call produces a different reaction, the group can protect itself from several kinds of danger.

Elephants produce deep rumbles, and many of these rumbles are infrasound, which means they are too low for human ears to hear. Low sounds like these can travel for several kilometers, which allows elephants to stay in contact with family members that are far away.

Honeybees communicate through movement. A bee that discovers flowers performs a special dance inside the hive, and the dance indicates which direction the other bees should fly and approximately how far they should travel.

Ants depend on smell. As an ant returns from a source of food, it deposits a chemical called a pheromone on the ground, and this scent forms a trail that other ants follow to the food.

The Arabian wolf inhabits the deserts and mountains of Saudi Arabia. A wolf howls to gather its pack together, and the howl also warns other wolves to stay out of the pack's territory, the area the pack occupies and defends.

Communication can also be risky, because a loud call that alerts relatives may also reveal the caller's location to a predator. For this reason, many animals must balance the benefits of sharing information against the danger of being noticed.

Animals send signals to warn of danger, to locate food, and to remain with their families. Scientists record these sounds with microphones and analyze them with computers, hoping to interpret more of the hidden conversations happening all around us.

versions.title: Hidden Conversations: How Animals Communicate
versions.text:
Although animals cannot speak in human language, many species have evolved remarkably sophisticated ways of exchanging information, and scientists who study these systems are continually working to interpret signals that once seemed like simple noise or random behavior.

Vervet monkeys, native to the savannas of Africa, offer one of the best-documented examples of distinct, predator-specific alarm calls. When a vervet spots a leopard, it gives one call, prompting troop members to scramble up into the trees, out of the big cat's reach. A different call, reserved for eagles, sends the group diving down into dense vegetation, away from the open sky where a bird of prey could strike. A third, distinct vocalization warns specifically of snakes, and causes nearby monkeys to rear up on their hind legs and scan the surrounding grass below. Each call triggers a different, appropriate escape response, showing that the monkeys are not merely expressing alarm but transmitting specific information about the nature of the threat.

Other animals, meanwhile, rely on signals entirely beyond the range of human hearing or perception. Elephants produce deep rumbling vocalizations that include infrasound, sound waves pitched too low for human ears to detect, which can travel for several kilometers across open terrain, allowing separated herd members to stay in contact over long distances. Honeybees, by contrast, communicate visually and physically: a forager returning to the hive performs a figure-eight dance whose angle and duration indicate the direction and distance of a nearby source of flowers. Ants, meanwhile, lay down pheromone trails, chemical signals deposited on the ground, which guide other members of the colony directly to food or alert them to danger along the path.

In the deserts and mountains of Saudi Arabia, the Arabian wolf uses long, carrying howls both to gather scattered pack members and to mark and defend its territory against rival wolves, a vocal strategy particularly suited to vast, open landscapes where visual signals alone would prove ineffective.

Communication of this kind is not without risk. A loud call that gathers the pack or warns of danger can simultaneously reveal an animal's exact location to a nearby predator, meaning that every vocalization carries a trade-off between the benefit of informing allies and the danger of being overheard by an enemy.

To study these hidden conversations, scientists record animal sounds with sensitive microphones and then analyze the recordings using computers capable of detecting patterns invisible to the human ear, gradually building a clearer picture of how creatures without language still manage to share urgent, detailed information with one another.

versions.title: Hidden Conversations: How Animals Communicate
versions.text:
Although animals possess nothing resembling human language, an increasing body of scientific research demonstrates that many species have evolved intricate systems for exchanging information, and researchers devoted to interpreting these systems are steadily uncovering complexity in behavior once dismissed as simple noise or instinctive reaction.

Vervet monkeys, native to the savannas of sub-Saharan Africa, provide one of the most thoroughly documented illustrations of distinct, predator-specific alarm calls. Upon sighting a leopard, a vervet emits one particular call, prompting troop members to scramble immediately into the trees, beyond the reach of the approaching cat. A separate, equally distinct vocalization, reserved specifically for eagles, sends the group diving down into dense ground-level vegetation, away from the open sky where a swooping bird of prey could otherwise strike unimpeded. A third call warns specifically of snakes, causing nearby monkeys to rear upright on their hind legs and scan the surrounding grass. Because each call provokes a markedly different, situationally appropriate escape response, researchers conclude that the monkeys are not merely expressing generalized alarm but are transmitting precise, categorized information about the nature of the approaching threat.

Other species rely on signals that lie entirely beyond the range of human perception. Elephants produce deep rumbling vocalizations incorporating infrasound, sound waves pitched too low for human ears to register, which can nonetheless propagate for several kilometers across open terrain, enabling geographically separated herd members to remain in continuous contact. Honeybees, in contrast, communicate through an elaborate visual and physical display: a forager returning from a successful outing performs a precise figure-eight dance whose angle relative to the sun and whose duration together encode the direction and distance of a newly discovered source of flowers. Ants, meanwhile, deposit pheromone trails, chemical signals released onto the ground, which subsequently guide fellow colony members directly toward food sources or warn them of danger encountered along a previously traveled path.

Across the deserts and mountainous terrain of Saudi Arabia, the Arabian wolf employs long, far-carrying howls to accomplish two distinct purposes simultaneously: gathering pack members who have become scattered during a hunt, and marking or actively defending territorial boundaries against rival wolves, a vocal strategy particularly well suited to vast, open landscapes where purely visual signaling would prove largely ineffective.

Communication of this nature, however, is never without inherent risk. A call loud enough to summon distant pack members or broadcast an imminent danger can simultaneously betray the calling animal's precise location to an opportunistic predator lurking nearby, meaning that virtually every vocalization embodies an unavoidable trade-off between the benefit of informing allies and the considerable danger of being overheard by an adversary.

To investigate these largely hidden conversations, scientists deploy sensitive microphones to record animal sounds across diverse habitats and subsequently analyze the resulting recordings using computer algorithms capable of detecting acoustic patterns entirely imperceptible to the unaided human ear, gradually assembling an increasingly detailed picture of how creatures lacking true language nonetheless manage to exchange urgent, highly specific information with one another.

MID.modelAnswer: Vervet monkeys communicate with sound by using a different alarm call to warn about each predator, while the Arabian wolf also communicates with sound by howling to call its pack together and defend its territory. Elephants, on the other hand, communicate with deep rumbles that are too low for humans to hear but can travel far to reach family members. All of these signals are alike because they use sound to send a message, but they are different because each sound warns of danger or location in its own particular way.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say animal signals are a kind of language. Using evidence from the article, explain whether you agree.
checklist: I supported it with at least two examples from the article.
I used precise words such as interpret, distinct, and vocalization.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that animal signals act like a kind of language, because each one carries a distinct meaning that other animals can interpret and act on. For example, vervet monkeys use a different vocalization for each predator, and the monkeys that hear it know exactly whether to climb a tree, dive into bushes, or check the ground, almost like understanding separate words. Honeybees communicate in an equally specific way through a dance that tells other bees which direction and how far to fly for flowers, showing that these signals convey real information rather than random noise.
